title: De Anima
author: Tertullian

passages.original: Visa est quidem sibi et ex sacris, quas putant, litteris hausisse, quia plerosque auctores etiam deos existimavit antiquitas, nedum divos, ut Mercurium Aegyptium, cui praecipue Plato adsuevit, ut Silenum Phrygem, cui a pastoribus perducto ingentes aures suas Midas tradidit, ut Hermotimum, cui Clazomenii mortuo templum contulerunt, ut Orpheum, ut Musaeum, ut Pherecydem Pythagorae magistrum. Quid autem, si philosophi etiam illa incursaverunt quae penes nos apocryphorum confessione damnantur, certos nihil recipiendum quod non conspiret germanae et ipso iam aevo pronatae propheticae paraturae, quando et pseudoprophetarum meminerimus et multo prius apostatarum spirituum, qui huiusmodi quoque ingeniorum calliditate omnem faciem saeculi instruxerint?
passages.english: It [philosophy] has indeed fancied that it drew [its ideas] even from what they consider sacred writings, because antiquity regarded many of its authors even as gods, let alone as deified men: such as the Egyptian Mercury, with whom Plato was especially familiar; such as the Phrygian Silenus, to whom, when he was brought to him by shepherds, Midas offered his own huge ears; such as Hermotimus, to whom the Clazomenians dedicated a temple after his death; such as Orpheus, such as Musaeus, such as Pherecydes, the teacher of Pythagoras. But what if the philosophers have also stumbled upon those writings which among us are condemned by being acknowledged as apocryphal, since we are certain that nothing is to be received which does not agree with the genuine prophetic provision, which came into being already in that very age, seeing that we remember both the false prophets and, much earlier, the apostate spirits, who have furnished the whole face of the world with the cunning of minds of this kind too?
passages.notes: 'Ingentes aures suas Midas tradidit' is obscure: literally 'Midas handed over his huge ears' (i.e. gave him an attentive hearing). 'Paraturae' (provision, equipment) is an unusual word; sense uncertain.

passages.original: Habuit et philosophia libertatem ingenii et medicina necessitatem artificii ad extendendos de anima retractatus; late quaeruntur incerta, latius disputantur praesumpta. Quanta difficultas probandi, tanta operositas suadendi, ut merito Heraclitus ille tenebrosus vastiores caligines animadvertens apud examinatores animae taedio quaestionum pronuntiarit terminos animae nequaquam invenisse omnem viam ingrediendo. Christiano autem paucis ad scientiam huius rei opus est.
passages.english: Both philosophy, with its freedom of intellect, and medicine, with the demands of its craft, have had [reason] to extend their treatments of the soul; uncertainties are inquired into widely, assumptions are debated more widely still. As great as the difficulty of proving is the labour of persuading, so that the famous obscure Heraclitus, observing the vaster darkness among the examiners of the soul, out of weariness with the questions rightly declared that he had by no means found the limits of the soul, though he travelled every road. But for the Christian few things are needed for knowledge of this matter.

passages.original: Alii immortalem negant animam, alii plusquam immortalem adfirmant, alii de substantia, alii de forma, alii de unaquaque dispositione disceptant, hi statum eius aliunde ducunt, hi exitum aliorsum abducunt, prout aut Platonis honor aut Zenonis vigor aut Aristotelis tenor aut Epicuri stupor aut Heracliti maeror aut Empedoclis furor persuaserunt. Deliquit, opinor, divina doctrina ex Iudaea potius quam ex Graecia oriens.
passages.english: Some deny that the soul is immortal, others assert that it is more than immortal; some dispute about its substance, others about its form, others about each of its arrangements; these derive its origin from one source, those lead its departure off to another place, according as the dignity of Plato, or the vigour of Zeno, or the steadiness of Aristotle, or the stupidity of Epicurus, or the gloom of Heraclitus, or the frenzy of Empedocles has persuaded them. The divine teaching, I suppose, was at fault in arising from Judaea rather than from Greece.

passages.original: Fortassean exstruentur magis ad auferendam animae corpulentiam, si non alios e contrario inspexerint, et quidem plures, corpus animae vindicantes. Nec illos dico solos qui eam de manifestis corporalibus effingunt, ut Hipparchus et Heraclitus ex igni, ut Hippon et Thales ex aqua, ut Empedocles et Critias ex sanguine, ut Epicurus ex atomis, si et atomi corpulentias de coitu suo cogunt, ut Critolaus et Peripatetici eius ex quinta nescio qua substantia, si et illa corpus, quia corpora includit, - sed etiam Stoicos allego, qui spiritum praedicantes animam paene nobiscum, qua proxima inter se flatus et spiritus, tamen corpus animam facile persuadebunt.
passages.english: Perhaps they will be drawn up in greater force to take away the corporeality of the soul, if they do not look at others on the opposite side, and indeed more numerous ones, who claim a body for the soul. And I do not mean only those who fashion it out of manifestly corporeal things: as Hipparchus and Heraclitus from fire, as Hippon and Thales from water, as Empedocles and Critias from blood, as Epicurus from atoms, if atoms too compel corporeal masses out of their coming together, as Critolaus and his Peripatetics from some fifth substance or other, if that too is a body, since it encloses bodies. But I also cite the Stoics, who, though they declare the soul to be spirit almost as we do, inasmuch as breath and spirit are very close to one another, will nevertheless easily persuade [us] that the soul is a body.
passages.notes: 'Hipparchus' is the manuscript name; it may stand for Hippasus, who is usually paired with Heraclitus as holding the soul to be fire. The opening sentence is elliptical; 'they' refers to the philosophers named in the preceding context.

passages.original: Quo, inquit, digresso animal emoritur, corpus est: consito autem spiritu digresso animal emoritur, ergo consitus spiritus corpus est; consitus autem spiritus anima est, ergo corpus est anima. Vult et Cleanthes non solum corporis lineamentis, sed et animae notis similitudinem parentibus in filios respondere, de speculo scilicet morum et ingeniorum et adfectuum, corporis autem similitudinem et dissimilitudinem capere et animam. Itaque corpus similitudini vel dissimilitudini obnoxium. Item corporalium et incorporalium passiones inter se non communicare. Porro et animam compati corpori, cui laeso ictibus, vulneribus, ulceribus condolescit, et corpus animae, cui adflictae cura, angore, amore cobaerescit per detrimentum socii vigoris, cuius pudorem et pavorem rubore atque pallore testetur.
passages.english: That, he says, at whose departure a living creature dies, is a body; but when the implanted breath departs, a living creature dies; therefore the implanted breath is a body; but the implanted breath is the soul; therefore the soul is a body. Cleanthes too holds that the likeness of parents is answered in their children not only in the features of the body but also in the marks of the soul, namely from the mirror of character, abilities and feelings; and that the soul also takes on likeness and unlikeness of the body. Therefore [the soul] is a body, subject to likeness or unlikeness. Again, [he holds] that the sufferings of corporeal and incorporeal things do not communicate with each other. But the soul suffers along with the body, grieving with it when it is hurt by blows, wounds and sores; and the body with the soul, being bound to it when it is afflicted by care, anguish or love, through the loss of their shared vigour, whose shame and fear it attests by blushing and pallor.
passages.notes: 'Cobaerescit' read as 'cohaerescit' (scanning error). The first sentence is Zeno's syllogism, continued from the preceding context.

passages.original: Pertinet ad statum fidei simplicem animam determinare secundum Platonem, id est uniformem, duntaxat substantiae nomine. Viderint artes et disciplinae, viderint et effigies. Quidam enim volunt aliam illi substantiam naturalem inesse spiritum, quasi aliud sit vivere, quod venit ab anima, aliud spirare, quod fiat a spiritu.
passages.english: It belongs to the standard of faith to define the soul as simple, according to Plato, that is, uniform, at least in respect of substance. Let arts and disciplines see to it, and let shapes [of the soul] see to it too. For some hold that there is within it another natural substance, the spirit, as though living, which comes from the soul, were one thing, and breathing, which is brought about by the spirit, another.
passages.notes: 'Viderint artes et disciplinae, viderint et effigies' is elliptical; sense uncertain.

passages.original: Dividitur autem in partes, nunc in duas a Platone, nunc in tres a Zenone, nunc in quinque et in sex a Panaetio, in septem a Sorano, etiam in octo penes Chrysippum, etiam in novem penes Apollophanem, sed et in duodecim apud quosdam Stoicorum, et in duas amplius apud Posidonium, qui a duobus exorsus titulis, principali, quod aiunt á¼¡Î³ÎµÎ¼Î¿Î½Î¹Îºá½¸Î½, et a rationali, quod aiunt Î»Î¿Î³Î¹Îºá½¸Î½, in decem et septem exinde prosecuit; ita aliae ex aliis species dividunt animam.
passages.english: Now [the soul] is divided into parts: now into two by Plato, now into three by Zeno, now into five and six by Panaetius, into seven by Soranus, even into eight in Chrysippus, even into nine in Apollophanes, and also into twelve among some of the Stoics, and into two more in Posidonius. He began from two headings, the ruling [part], which they call the *hēgemonikon*, and the rational [part], which they call the *logikon*, and from there cut it up into seventeen. So different classes divide the soul, some from others.
passages.notes: Greek terms restored from mojibake: ἡγεμονικόν and λογικόν. 'Into two more' (in duas amplius) is unclear; it may mean two more than the twelve, that is fourteen.

passages.original: Si enim scrutatorem et dispectorem cordis deum legimus, si etiam prophetes eius occulta cordis traducendo probatur, si deus ipse recogitatus cordis in populo praevenit, Quid cogitatis in cordibus vestris nequam? si et David, Cor mundum conde in me deus, et Paulus corde ait credi in iustitiam, et Ioannes corde ait suo unumquemque reprehendi, si postremo qui viderit feminam ad concupiscendum, iam adulteravit in corde, simul utrumque dilucet, et esse principale in anima, quod intentio divina conveniat, id est vim sapientialem atque vitalem (quod enim sapit, vividum est), et in eo thesauro corporis haberi ad quem deus respicit, ut neque extrinsecus agitari putes principale istud secundum Heraclitum, neque per totum corpus ventilari secundum Moschionem, neque in capite concludi secundum Platonem, neque in vertice potius praesidere secundum Xenocratem, neque in cerebro cubare secundum Hippocraten, sed nec circa cerebri fundamentum, ut Herophilus, nec in membranulis, ut Strato et Erasistratus, nec in superciliorum meditullio, ut Strato Physicus, nec in tota lorica pectoris, ut Epicurus, sed quod et Aegyptii renuntiaverunt, et qui divinarum commentatores videbantur, ut et ille versus Orphei vel Empedoclis: Namque homini sanguis circumcordialis est sensus. Etiam Protagoras, etiam Apollodorus et Chrysippus haec sapiunt, ut vel ab istis retusus Asclepiades capras suas quaerat sine corde balantes et muscas suas abigat sine capite volitantes, et omnes iam sciant se potius sine corde et cerebro vivere qui dispositionem animae humanae de condicione bestiarum praeiudicarint.
passages.english: For if we read that God is the searcher and discerner of the heart; if his prophet too is proved [a prophet] by exposing the secrets of the heart; if God himself anticipates the thoughts of the heart in the people, [saying] 'Why do you think evil in your hearts?'; if David also [says], 'Create a clean heart in me, O God,' and Paul says that one believes with the heart unto righteousness, and John says that each person is condemned by his own heart; if, finally, whoever has looked at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery in his heart: then two things together become clear. [First,] there is a ruling part in the soul, to which the divine attention is directed, that is, a power of wisdom and of life (for what has wisdom is alive). [Second,] it is held in that treasure-house of the body to which God looks. So you should not think that this ruling part is stirred from outside, as Heraclitus [held]; nor that it is blown through the whole body, as Moschion [held]; nor that it is enclosed in the head, as Plato [held]; nor that it presides rather in the crown of the head, as Xenocrates [held]; nor that it lies in the brain, as Hippocrates [held]. Nor is it around the base of the brain, as Herophilus [held]; nor in the membranes, as Strato and Erasistratus [held]; nor in the midpoint between the eyebrows, as Strato the Physicist [held]; nor in the whole breastplate of the chest, as Epicurus [held]. [It is] rather what the Egyptians too have declared, and those who were regarded as interpreters of divine things, as in that verse of Orpheus or Empedocles: 'For in man the blood around the heart is sense.' Protagoras too, and Apollodorus and Chrysippus, think this. So, beaten back even by these, Asclepiades may go looking for his goats bleating without a heart and drive off his flies flying about without a head. And let all now know that it is rather they who live without heart and brain who have prejudged the arrangement of the human soul from the condition of beasts.
passages.notes: Strato is named twice, once with Erasistratus and once as 'Strato the Physicist'; the text may be corrupt at one of these points.

passages.original: Inrationale autem posterius intellegendum est, ut quod acciderit ex serpentis instinctu, ipsum illud transgressionis admissum, atque exinde inoleverit et coadoleverit in anima ad instar iam naturalitatis, quia statim in naturae primordio accidit. Ceterum cum idem Plato solum rationale dicat, ut in anima dei ipsius, si nos etiam inrationale naturae adscripserimus, quam a deo anima nostra sortita est, aeque inrationale de deo erit, utpote naturale, quia naturae deus auctor est. Sed enim a diabolo immissio delicti, inrationale autem omne delictum, igitur a diabolo inrationale, a quo et delictum, extraneum a deo, a quo est inrationale alienum.
passages.english: The irrational, however, must be understood as later, as something that arose from the serpent's prompting, namely that very commission of the transgression, and thereafter grew into and grew up together with the soul so as to resemble something natural, because it happened immediately at the beginning of [human] nature. Moreover, since the same Plato calls only the rational [part] that in the soul of God himself, if we were also to ascribe the irrational to the nature which our soul received from God, the irrational would equally come from God, as being natural, because God is the author of nature. But the prompting to sin is from the devil, and all sin is irrational; therefore the irrational is from the devil, from whom sin also comes, foreign to God, to whom the irrational is alien.

passages.original: Convetor ad intellectualium partem, quemadmodum illam Plato a corporalibus separatam haereticis commendaverit, agnitionem ante mortem consecutus. Ait enim in Phaedone: Quid tum erga ipsam prudentiae possessionem? Utrumne impedimentum erit corpus, an non, si quis illud socium assumpserit in quaestionem?
passages.english: I turn to the part concerning intellectual things, how Plato, having separated it from bodily things, commended it to the heretics, having attained knowledge before death. For he says in the Phaedo: 'What then about the very possession of wisdom? Will the body be a hindrance or not, if one takes it as a partner in the inquiry?'

passages.original: Proinde enim viam sternunt postea inducendi eius, sicut et animi, a quo scilicet proveniat intellectus. Volunt infantiam sola anima contineri, qua tantummodo vivat, non ut pariter sapiat, quia nec omnia sapiant quae vivant. Denique arbores vivere, nec tamen sapere, secundum Aristotelem, et si quis alius substantiam animalem in universa communicat, quae apud nos in homine privata res est, non modo ut dei opus, quod et cetera, sed ut dei flatus, quod haec sola quam dicimus cum omni instructu suo nasci.
passages.english: For they are in fact paving the way for introducing it later, as also the mind, from which, of course, intellect is supposed to come. They hold that infancy is maintained by the soul alone, by which it merely lives, not so that it also has understanding, since not all things that live have understanding. Thus trees live, yet do not understand, according to Aristotle, and anyone else who shares the animate substance among all things, whereas with us it is something peculiar to man, not only as the work of God, which other things are too, but as the breath of God, which this alone is; [the soul] which we say is born with its full equipment.
passages.notes: The final clause is syntactically difficult; 'quod haec sola quam dicimus cum omni instructu suo nasci' seems corrupt or compressed. Rendered as: the soul alone is God's breath, and we say it is born with all its faculties.

passages.original: Et hic itaque concludimus omnia naturalia animae ut substantiva eius ipsi inesse et cum ipsa procedere atque proficere, ex quo ipsa censetur. Sicut et Seneca saepe noster: Insita sunt nobis omnium artium et aetatum semina, magisterque ex occulto deus producit ingenia, ex seminibus scilicet insitis et occultis per infantiam, quae sunt et intellectus. Ex his enim producuntur ingenia. Porro et frugum seminibus una generis cuiusque forma est, processus tamen varii, alia integro statu evadunt, alia etiam meliora respondent, alia degenerant pro condicione caeli et soli, pro ratione operis et curae, pro temporum eventu, pro licentia casuum: ita et animam licebit semine uniformem, fetu multiformem.
passages.english: And here, therefore, we conclude that all the natural properties of the soul are inherent in it as belonging to its substance, and that they advance and develop with it from the moment it is itself reckoned [as existing]. As our Seneca often [says]: 'The seeds of all arts and ages are implanted in us, and God, the hidden teacher, draws out our talents', that is, from the seeds implanted and hidden through infancy, which are also the intellect. For from these talents are drawn out. Further, the seeds of crops too have a single form for each kind, yet varied developments: some come out in sound condition, some even turn out better, some degenerate, according to the condition of climate and soil, the method of labour and care, the course of the seasons, the licence of chance. So too it will be possible for the soul to be uniform in seed, multiform in offspring.

passages.original: Nam et hic etiam de locis interest. Thebis hebetes et brutos nasci relatum est, Athenis sapiendi dicendique acutissimos; ubi penes Colyttum pueri mense citius eloquuntur praecoca lingua. Siquidem et Plato in Timaeo Minervam affirmat, cum urbem illam moliretur, nihil aliud quam regionis naturam prospexisse, talia ingenia pollicitam, unde et ipse in Legibus Megillo et Cliniae praecipit condendae civitati locum procurare. Sed Empedocles causam argutae indolis et obtusae in sanguinis qualitate constituit;
passages.english: For here too the place makes a difference. It is reported that at Thebes people are born dull and stupid, at Athens most acute in wisdom and speech; there, at Colyttus, children speak a month earlier with precocious tongues. Indeed Plato too, in the Timaeus, affirms that Minerva, when she was founding that city, considered nothing but the nature of the region, which promised such talents; whence he himself also, in the Laws, instructs Megillus and Clinias to take care over the site for founding their city. But Empedocles places the cause of a sharp or dull disposition in the quality of the blood;
passages.notes: The passage ends mid-sentence; the clause continues in the following context.

passages.original: Quidam de caelis devenisse se credunt, tanta persuasione quanta et illuc indubitate regressuros repromittunt, ut Saturninus Menandri Simoniani discipulus induxit, hominem affirmans ab angelis factum primoque opus futile et invalidum et instabile in terra vermis instar palpitasse, quod consistendi vires deessent, dehinc ex misericordia summae potestatis, ad cuius effigiem nec tamen plene perspectam temere structus fuisset, scintillulam vitae consecutum, quae illud exsuscitarit et erexerit et constantius animarit et post decessum vitae ad matricem relatura sit.
passages.english: Some believe that they have come down from the heavens, with as much conviction as that with which they promise that they will undoubtedly return there; as Saturninus, disciple of Menander the Simonian, taught, affirming that man was made by angels, and at first, a futile, feeble and unstable work, he wriggled on the earth like a worm, because he lacked the strength to stand; then, through the mercy of the supreme power, in whose image (though not fully perceived) he had been rashly constructed, he obtained a little spark of life, which roused him, raised him up, animated him more firmly, and after his departure from life will carry [him] back to its source.

passages.original: Magnae autem ac multae differentiae corporum pro gentilitate, pro magnitudine, pro habitudine, pro aetate, pro valetudine. Num ergo et oblivionum differentiae aestimabuntur? Sed uniformis oblivio est; ergo non erit corporalitas multiformis in causa exitus uniformis. Multa item documenta, teste ipso Platone, divinationem animae probaverunt, quae proposuimus iam Hermogeni. Sed nec quisquam hominum non et ipse aliquando praesagam animam suam sentit, aut ominis aut periculi aut gaudii augurem. Si divinationi non obstrepit corpus, nec memoriae opinor officiet.
passages.english: Yet the differences between bodies are great and many, according to race, size, condition, age and health. Are we then also to reckon differences of forgetting? But forgetting is uniform; therefore a multiform bodiliness will not be the cause of a uniform outcome. Again, many proofs, as Plato himself testifies, have established the soul's power of divination, which we have already set out against Hermogenes. Indeed there is no one among men who does not himself at some time sense that his soul is presaging, a foreteller of some omen, or danger, or joy. If the body does not obstruct divination, neither, I think, will it hinder memory.
passages.notes: The reference is to Tertullian's work against Hermogenes (possibly the lost De censu animae).

passages.original: eam editam, et de uteri fornace fumantem et calore solutam, ut ferrum ignitum et ibidem frigidae immersum, ita aÃ«ris rigore percussam et vim animalem rapere et vocalem sonum reddere. Hoc Stoici cum Aenesidemo, et ipse interdum Plato, cum dicit perinde animam extraneam alias et extorrem uteri prima adspiratione nascentis infantis adduci, sicut exspiratione novissima educi. Videbimus an sententiam finxerit. Ne ex medicis quidem defuit Hicesius, et naturae et artis suae praevaricator.
passages.english: [they hold that] once it has been brought forth, steaming from the furnace of the womb and loosened by heat, like red-hot iron plunged there and then into cold water, so, struck by the chill of the air, it both seizes the animal force and gives out vocal sound. This is held by the Stoics together with Aenesidemus, and at times by Plato himself, when he says that the soul, otherwise foreign and exiled from the womb, is drawn in with the first breath of the infant being born, just as it is drawn out with the last exhalation. We shall see whether he made up this opinion. Not even among the physicians was Hicesius lacking, a betrayer both of nature and of his own art.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence; the subject ('it', the fetus/seed of flesh) and governing verb lie in the preceding context. 'aÃ«ris' is an encoding error for 'aëris'.

passages.original: Quodsi qui, ut Plato, perinde non putat duas animas in unum convenire, sicut nec corpora, ego illi non modo duas animas in unum congestas ostendissem, sicut et corpora, in fetibus, verum et alia multa cum anima conserta, daemonis scilicet, nec unius, ut in Socrate ipso, verum et septenarii spiritus, ut in Magdalena, et legionarii numeri, ut in Geraseno, quo facilius anima cum anima conseretur ex societate substantiae quam spiritus nequam ex diversitate naturae.
passages.english: But if anyone, like Plato, does not think that two souls come together into one, any more than bodies do, I would show him not only two souls gathered into one, as bodies are too, in unborn children, but also many other things joined with the soul: demons, that is, and not just one, as in Socrates himself, but also a sevenfold spirit, as in the Magdalene, and one of legionary number, as in the Gerasene. All the more easily, then, will soul be joined with soul through sharing a substance than evil spirits [are joined with a soul] across a difference of nature.

passages.original: At idem in sexto Legum monens cavere ne vitiatio seminis ex aliqua vilitate concubitus labem corpori et animae supparet, nescio de pristina magis, an de ista sententia sibi exciderit. Ostendit enim animam de semine induci, quod curari monet, non de prima aspiratione nascentis. Unde, oro te, similitudine animae quoque parentibus de ingeniis respondemus secundum Cleanthis testimonium, si non et ex animae semine educimur? Cur autem et veteres astrologi genituram hominis ab initio conceptus digerebant, si non exinde et anima est? Ad quam aeque pertinet, si quid est, flatus.
passages.english: But the same [Plato], in the sixth [book] of the Laws, warning [us] to take care lest corruption of the seed from some baseness of intercourse should cause a stain to body and soul, has let slip from himself — I do not know whether rather his earlier opinion or this one. For he shows that the soul is brought in from the seed, which he warns should be cared for, not from the first breath of the one being born. Whence, I ask you, do we also correspond to our parents in character by likeness of soul, according to the testimony of Cleanthes, if we are not also brought forth from the seed of the soul? And why did the ancient astrologers too reckon a person's nativity from the beginning of conception, if the soul too is not from then? To it, equally, the breath belongs, if it is anything.
passages.notes: 'supparet' is an unusual form (perhaps 'subparet', 'cause/produce'); sense inferred.

passages.original: Sed et quid utique de solo Graeciae censu, ut non ex omni gente, et ex omni aetate ac dignitate, ex omni denique sexu, Î¼ÎµÏÎµÎ¼ÏÏ Ïá½½ÏÎµÎ¹Ï et Î¼ÎµÏÎµÎ½ÏÏÎ¼Î±Ïá½½ÏÎµÎ¹Ï quotidie existant, cur solus Pythagoras alium atque alium se recognoscat, non et ego? aut si privilegium philosophorum est, et utique Graecorum, quasi non et Scythae et ludi philosophentur, cur neminem se retro meminit Epicurus, neminem Chrysippus, neminem Zeno, ne ipse quidem Plato, quem forsitan Nestorem credidissemus ob mella facundiae?
passages.english: But why, in any case, [speak] only of the census of Greece — as though people transformed and re-embodied did not daily appear from every nation, from every age and rank, in short from every sex? Why does Pythagoras alone recognise himself as one person after another, and not I as well? Or if it is a privilege of philosophers, and of Greeks at that — as though Scythians and Indians did not also philosophise — why does Epicurus remember himself as no one in the past, Chrysippus as no one, Zeno as no one, not even Plato himself, whom we might perhaps have believed to be Nestor on account of the honey of his eloquence?
passages.notes: The Greek words are garbled by encoding; read as μεταμορφούμενοι ('transformed') and μετενσωματούμενοι ('re-embodied'). 'ludi' is a scanning error for 'Indi' (Indians).

passages.original: Nam et qui laboribus atque servitiis puniendi in asinos utique et mulos recorporabuntur, quantum sibi de pistrinis et aquilegis rotis gratulabuntur, si metallorum et ergastulorum et operum publicorum ipsorumque carcerum, licet otiosorum, recordentur! Perinde qui integre morati commendaverint iudici vitam, quaero praemia, sed potius invenio supplicia. Nimirum magna merces bonis in animalia quaecunque restitui. Pavum se meminit Homerus Ennio somniante: sed poetis nec vigilantibus credam. Etsi pulcherrimus pavus et quo velit colore cultissimus: sed tacent pennae, sed displicet vox, et poetae nihil aliud quam cantare malunt. Damnatus est igitur Homerus in pavum, non honoratus.
passages.english: For those too who are to be punished with labours and servitude will surely be re-embodied as asses and mules. How they will congratulate themselves on the mills and the water-wheels, if they remember the mines and the workhouses and the public works and the prisons themselves, idle though these are! Likewise, for those of upright character who have commended their life to the judge, I look for rewards, but I find punishments instead. A great payment indeed for the good, to be restored into animals of any kind! Homer remembered being a peacock, as Ennius dreamed; but I would not trust poets even when they are awake. Granted, the peacock is most beautiful and most finely adorned in whatever colour it likes; but its feathers are silent, its voice is unpleasant, and poets want nothing more than to sing. So Homer was condemned into a peacock, not honoured.

passages.original: Nulla quidem ad hodiernum dementiae huiusmodi sententia erupit sub nomine haeretico quae humanas animas refingat in bestias. Sed necessarie hanc quoque speciem intulimus et exclusimus ut superioribus cohaerentem, quo perinde in pavo retunderetur Homerus sicut in Pythagora Euphorbus, atque ita hac etiam metempsychosi sive metensomatosi repercussa illa rursus caederetur quae aliquid haereticis sumministravit. Nam et Simon Samarites in Actis Apostolorum redemptor spiritus sancti, posteaquam damnatus ab ipso cum pecunia sua interitum frustra flevit, conversus ad veritatis expugnationem quasi pro solatio ultionis, fultus etiam artis suae viribus, ad praestigias virtutis alicuius, Helenen quandam Tyriam de loco libidinis publicae eadem pecunia redemit, dignam sibi mercedem pro spiritu sancto.
passages.english: No opinion of madness of this kind has, up to today, broken out under a heretical name that would refashion human souls into beasts. But we necessarily brought in this form too and excluded it, as cohering with the preceding, so that Homer might be beaten back in the peacock just as Euphorbus in Pythagoras, and so that, with this metempsychosis or metensomatosis also repelled, that other [doctrine] might again be struck down which has supplied something to the heretics. For Simon the Samaritan too, in the Acts of the Apostles, the would-be purchaser of the Holy Spirit, after he had been condemned by [Peter] himself, together with his money, and had vainly wept over his ruin, turned to assaulting the truth as if for the consolation of revenge, and, supported also by the powers of his art, for the illusions of some power, he bought with that same money a certain Helen of Tyre from a place of public lust, a reward worthy of him in place of the Holy Spirit.
passages.notes: 'ab ipso' presumably refers to Peter. 'redemptor' here means would-be buyer.

passages.original: At illo ei dedit passionem cuius est actio. Quodsi hominis est pati mortem dissolutricem corporis et peremptricem sensus, quam ineptum ut tanta vis ad hominem non pertinere dicatur. Multo coactius Seneca, Post mortem, ait, omnia finiuntur, etiam ipsa. Hoc si ita est, iam et mors ad semetipsam pertinebit, si et ipsa finitur; eo magis ad hominem, in quo inter omnia finiendo et ipsa finitur. Mors nihil ad nos, ergo et vita nihil ad nos.
passages.english: But he gave it the experiencing to which the action belongs. Now if it belongs to man to suffer death, which dissolves the body and destroys sensation, how absurd that so great a force should be said not to concern man. Much more cogently Seneca says: 'After death everything is ended, even [death] itself.' If this is so, then death too will concern itself, if it too is ended; all the more will it concern man, in whom, among all things being ended, it itself too is ended. [If] death is nothing to us, then life too is nothing to us.
passages.notes: First sentence obscure: 'illo' likely 'illi' (to man); sense is that the one who acts (dies) is the one who suffers death.

passages.original: Quis autem tam extraneus humanitatis ut non aliquam aliquando visionem fidelem senserit? Pauca de insignioribus perstringens Epicuro pudorem imperabo. Astyages Medorum regnator quod filiae Mandanae adhuc virginis vesicam in diluvionem Asiae fluxisse somnio viderit Herodotus refert; item anno post nuptias eius ex isdem locis vitem exortam toti Asiae incubasse. Hoc etiam Charon Lampsacenus Herodoto prior tradit. Qui filium eius tanto operi interpretati sunt, non fefellerunt;
passages.english: And who is so foreign to humanity as never at some time to have experienced some trustworthy vision? Touching briefly on a few of the more notable, I shall command Epicurus to be ashamed. Herodotus reports that Astyages, ruler of the Medes, saw in a dream that the bladder of his daughter Mandane, still a virgin, flowed out into a flood over Asia; likewise, a year after her marriage, that a vine sprang up from the same parts and overspread all Asia. Charon of Lampsacus, earlier than Herodotus, also relates this. Those who interpreted her son [as destined] for so great a work were not mistaken;

passages.original: Sicut ergo dignatio dei et in ethnicos, ita et temptatio mali in sanctos, a quibus nec interdiu absistit, ut vel dormientibus obrepat qua potest, si vigilantibus non potest. Tertia species erunt somnia quae sibimet ipsa anima videtur inducere ex intentione circumstantiarum. Porro quoniam non est ex arbitrio somniare (nam et Epicharmus ita sentit), quomodo ipsa erit sibi causa alicuius visionis? Num ergo haec species naturali formae relinquenda est, servans animae etiam in ecstasi res suas perpeti? Ea autem, quae neque a deo neque a daemonio neque ab anima videbuntur accidere, et praeter opinionem et praeter interpretationem et praeter enarrationem facultatis, ipsi proprie ecstasi et rationi eius separabuntur.
passages.english: Just as, therefore, the favour of God [extends] even to the heathen, so too the temptation of evil [extends] to the saints, from whom it does not withdraw even by day, so that it creeps upon them while asleep in whatever way it can, if it cannot while they are awake. The third kind will be the dreams which the soul seems to bring upon itself from its attention to its circumstances. But since dreaming is not a matter of choice (Epicharmus too holds this view), how will [the soul] itself be the cause of any vision for itself? Should this kind, then, be left to the natural form, preserving for the soul, even in ecstasy, the undergoing of its own concerns? But those [dreams] which will seem to happen neither from God nor from a demon nor from the soul, and beyond expectation, beyond interpretation and beyond the capacity to recount, will be assigned properly to ecstasy itself and its nature.

passages.original: Sed quidam ad immortalitatem animae, quam quidem non a deo edocti infirme tuentur, ita argumentationes emendicant, ut velint credi etiam post mortem quasdam animas adhaerere corporibus. Ad hoc enim et Plato, etsi quas vult animas ad caelum statim expedit, in Politia tamen cuiusdam insepulti cadaver opponit longo tempore sine ulla labe prae animae scilicet individuitate servatum. Ad hoc et Democritus crementa unguium et comarum in sepulturis aliquanti temporis denotat.
passages.english: But certain people, in support of the immortality of the soul — which, not being taught by God, they defend feebly — beg for arguments in such a way that they want it believed that even after death certain souls cling to bodies. For to this end Plato too, although he dispatches the souls he wishes straight to heaven, nevertheless in the Republic sets forth the corpse of a certain unburied man preserved for a long time without any decay, on account, of course, of the soul's not being separated. To this end Democritus too notes the growth of nails and hair in graves for some time.

passages.original: Nam etsi prae gaudio quis spiritum exhalet, ut Chilon Spartanus, dum victorem Olympiae filium amplectitur, etsi prae gloria, ut Clidemus Atheniensis, dum ob historici stili praestantiam auro coronatur, etsi per somnium, ut Plato, etsi per risum, ut P. Crassus, multo violentior mors quae per aliena grassatur, quae animam per commoda expellit, quae tunc mori affert cum iocundius vivere est in exultatione, in honore, in requie, in voluptate.
passages.english: For even if someone breathes out his spirit from joy, like Chilon the Spartan while embracing his son, a victor at Olympia; even if from glory, like Clidemus the Athenian while being crowned with gold for the excellence of his historical style; even if in sleep, like Plato; even if through laughter, like P. Crassus — far more violent is the death that proceeds through things alien [to it], that drives out the soul through blessings, that brings dying at the very time when living is more delightful, in exultation, in honour, in rest, in pleasure.

passages.original: Quo igitur deducetur anima iam hinc reddimus. Omnes ferme philosophi, qui immortalitatem animae, qualiterqualiter volunt, tamen vindicant, ut Pythagoras, ut Empedocles, ut Plato, quique aliquod illi tempus indulgent ab excessu usque in conflagrationem universitatis, ut Stoici, suas solas, id est sapientum, animas in supernis mansionibus collocant. Plato quidem non temere philosophorum animabus hoc praestat, sed eorum qui philosophiam scilicet exornaverint amore puerorum. Adeo etiam inter philosophos magnum habet privilegium impuritas. Itaque apud illum in aetherem sublimantur animae sapientes, apud Arium in aÃ«rem, apud Stoicos sub lunam. Quos quidem miror quod imprudentes animas circa terram prosternant, cum illas a sapientibus multo superioribus erudiri affirment. Ubi erit scholae regio in tanta distantia diversoriorum?
passages.english: Where, then, the soul will be led, we now set out from here on. Nearly all the philosophers who affirm the immortality of the soul, in whatever way they mean it, such as Pythagoras, Empedocles and Plato, and those who grant it some time from its departure until the conflagration of the universe, such as the Stoics, place only their own souls, that is, the souls of the wise, in the upper dwellings. Plato indeed does not grant this indiscriminately to the souls of philosophers, but only to those who have, of course, adorned philosophy with the love of boys. So great a privilege does impurity hold even among philosophers! And so in his view wise souls are raised up into the ether, in Arius' view into the air, in the Stoics' view to beneath the moon. I am surprised at them, that they lay the unwise souls low around the earth, while they assert that these are taught by the wise, who are far above them. Where will the school be located, with so great a distance between the lodgings?
passages.notes: 'Arius' is probably Arius Didymus, the Stoic doxographer, but the identification is uncertain.

passages.original: Et ideo per quem visurum se credidit, vidit, quia per quem vidit, et credidit. Si et de nocturnis imaginibus opponitur saepe non frustra mortuos visos (nam et Nasamonas propria oracula apud parentum sepulchra mansitando captare, ut Heraclides scribit vel Nymphodorus vel Herodotus, et Celtas apud virorum fortium busta eadem de causa abnoctare, ut Nicander affirmat), non magis mortuos vere patimur in somnis quam vivos, sed eadem ratione mortuos qua et vivos et omnia quae videntur.
passages.english: And so he saw [it] through the one through whom he believed he would see, because he also believed through the one through whom he saw. If it is also objected, regarding images in the night, that the dead have often been seen, and not in vain (for the Nasamones obtain their own oracles by staying at the tombs of their parents, as Heraclides writes, or Nymphodorus, or Herodotus, and the Celts spend the night at the burial-mounds of brave men for the same reason, as Nicander affirms), we no more truly experience the dead in dreams than the living, but [we experience] the dead in the same way as the living and all things that are seen.
passages.notes: The opening sentence is compressed: Saul saw [the apparition] through the very spirit through whom he believed he would see it, because he believed through the same spirit through whom he saw. 'Non frustra' may mean 'not without reason' or 'not without effect'. The Latin construction of 'patimur' with 'mortuos' is loose; 'experience' is an interpretation.
